description: Looking forward to analyze open water and sea state images by grayscale segmentation
summary:
The problem: Floods, irrigation and wetlands change from week to week, but cloud and night hide the ground from optical satellites. Radar sees through both. The catch is that a radar image is not a water map: it is a picture of how rough each surface is. Turning it into an honest answer for a non-expert is the challenge.
The data: NISAR
NISAR (NASA-ISRO) is an L-band SAR mission. Its L2 GCOV product gives calibrated
backscatter on a 10 m map grid, in two polarisations (HH and HV), on a repeat track. Same place, same geometry, about every 12 days. Our test pair: Chokwe, Mozambique (Limpopo floodplain), 5 and 17 Jan 2026. These are BETA products.
The physics in one sentence
Calm water is a mirror: the radar pulse bounces away and the pixel turns black. Rough land scatters energy back and the pixel stays bright. So black means smooth. Smooth is usually water, but can also be tarmac, sand, or a freshly levelled field. Wet soil gets brighter, not darker.

What the real data showed
154 km2 became newly dark, with a genuine drop of about 10 dB, even after correcting
a +3.7 dB calibration offset between the two products.
Persistent water sits on low ground, as expected.
The new dark area mostly does not (enrichment 0.72), so the app flags it as "not flood-like". Irrigation ponding or field smoothing are plausible alternatives that still need optical confirmation.
details:
The problem

Floods, irrigation and wetlands change from week to week, but cloud and night hide the ground from optical satellites. Radar sees through both. The catch is that a radar image is not a water map: it is a picture of how rough each surface is. Turning it into an honest answer for a non-expert is the challenge.

The data: NISAR

NISAR (NASA-ISRO) is an L-band SAR mission. Its L2 GCOV product gives calibrated

backscatter on a 10 m map grid, in two polarisations (HH and HV), on a repeat track. Same place, same geometry, about every 12 days. Our test pair: Chokwe, Mozambique (Limpopo floodplain), 5 and 17 Jan 2026. These are BETA products.

The physics in one sentence

Calm water is a mirror: the radar pulse bounces away and the pixel turns black. Rough land scatters energy back and the pixel stays bright. So black means smooth. Smooth is usually water, but can also be tarmac, sand, or a freshly levelled field. Wet soil gets brighter, not darker.

What our app does

1. Scores each pixel. It fits a dark/bright mixture to each scene and reports a water-

likeness probability. The user sees a category and the reason for it, not just a number.

2. Adds context evidence. Terrain (slope and height above the nearest low ground, from

SRTM), thermal data (ECOSTRESS/Landsat, when it overlaps), and the earlier date's

evidence.

3. Compares two dates honestly. It orders them automatically, checks that they come

from the same track, frame and product version, and measures any calibration offset.

It then maps expansion, recession and persistent water.

4. Checks itself. It tests whether new water sits on low ground, as a flood should.

5. Exports to QGIS. GeoTIFF layers and styles, plus a manifest that records every

assumption.

What the real data showed

154 km2 became newly dark, with a genuine drop of about 10 dB, even after correcting

a +3.7 dB calibration offset between the two products.

Persistent water sits on low ground, as expected.


The new dark area mostly does not (enrichment 0.72), so the app flags it as "not flood-

like". Irrigation ponding or field smoothing are plausible alternatives that still need

optical confirmation.

Why it matters

Most demos colour a map and stop. Ours tells you how far to trust each pixel, why it is

dark, and when its own result does not make physical sense. That is what a decision-

maker needs before sending help.

Honest limits

The products are BETA and the results are unvalidated against ground truth.

SRTM elevation dates from 2000 and has metres of vertical noise.

Thermal data rarely matches the radar overpass time.

Co-registration between dates is not independently verified.
